turns.t: Doctor, I'll be direct, because I'm at the end of my rope. Walter has been up wandering the house at night, and I'm not sleeping.
I'm sorry to hear it. Walter, what do you make of it?
I get up for a stretch, that's all. It's been a week, one week, maybe.
It's three weeks, Walter. I've counted. The first night was the Thursday after his birthday.
So, one week from your side, three from Mrs Pearce's side. I'll write that down as one to three weeks. What does he do when he's up?
He goes to the front door and tries the handle. Or he goes into the kitchen and opens every cupboard.
I'm looking for something. I forget what.
Has he had any falls on his night walks?
No falls. He's steady, I always hear him and go down.
Is there anyone in the family with memory trouble?
His mother had it, in her eighties. Walter's seventy-nine.
I see. Walter, can you walk across the room for me? ~
Of course.
He walks steadily, turns well, and doesn't need to hold on to anything.
That's him in the day. It's the night that's the trouble. ~
It often is. Evenings and nights are hard for people whose memory is changing. ~
What can I do? ~
A few practical things. Keep the house well lit at night, with a lamp in the hall and the bathroom, and keep a regular bedtime.
We have a regular bedtime. It's the three o'clock wanders. ~
Then a simple alarm on the front door, a bell or a chime, so you wake when he tries it. And lock away anything unsafe.
I can get a chime. ~
Walter, do you nap in the day? ~
A bit. After lunch. ~
Try keeping the naps short, and get some daylight and a walk in the morning.
He'd like that. ~
Mrs Pearce, you need support as well. I'm going to refer you both to the community team for older people, who can talk about respite and what's available.
Thank you. I've been afraid to ask. ~
Please don't be. Ring us anytime. ~
Thank you, doctor. ~
I'd like to help her sleep better, doctor. ~
Then you're both doing the right thing by coming in. ~

chief_complaint.value: Walter has been up wandering the house at night

clinical_actions.description: Refer to community older people's team for support and respite
Keep the house lit at night with a regular bedtime
Fit a door chime alarm and lock away unsafe items
Keep daytime naps short; morning daylight and a walk

clinical_uncertainties.description: Patient says the night wandering has lasted one week; carer says three weeks; summarised by the doctor as one to three weeks, not confirmed.

contradictions_detected: Duration of night wandering: patient one week vs caregiver three weeks (approximate range only).
